lead.headline: Software Steps Into the Spotlight
lead.dek: TIME puts the programs inside the machine on its April 16 cover as applications, compatibility and ease of use begin deciding the personal-computer contest.
body: The personal-computer business has spent years selling the wonder of the machine itself. This week, the spotlight swings decisively to the programs that make those machines useful. TIME’s April 16 cover story, “The Wizard Inside the Machine,” calls software the magic carpet to the future and captures an industry learning that specifications alone do not close the sale.

That change can be seen on every shelf. Buyers now ask whether a computer can write a letter, keep accounts, draw a picture, teach a lesson or play the latest game—and whether files and programs will travel with them to the next machine. The contest is becoming one of libraries, compatibility and interfaces as much as processors and memory.

PC Magazine’s April 17 issue documents the application-rich IBM-compatible side of the market, while April’s COMPUTE! reaches across Commodore, Atari, Apple and IBM systems with ready-to-run programs. Together they show software becoming both the common language and the great dividing line of home computing.

For makers, the lesson is plain: a handsome box may win a demonstration, but a healthy catalog wins a household. For users, this new emphasis promises more practical machines—provided competing formats, disks and operating systems do not turn abundance into confusion.

stories.headline: Macintosh Meets the User-Group Crowd
body: COMPUTE! brings Apple’s new Macintosh before home-computer readers through a report on its Boston Computer Society demonstration. The compact 20-pound machine pairs an 8 MHz Motorola 68000 with a mouse, menus and a crisp graphical display.

The interface earns praise for direct manipulation, an Undo command and a remarkably tidy desktop. Yet the report also asks the question that follows every dazzling demonstration: what indispensable job will persuade ordinary buyers to spend $2,495?

MacWrite and MacPaint offer the first answer, turning words and pictures into visible objects on screen. The larger test will be whether independent developers can build a software shelf broad enough to make the unusual machine a standard.

stories.headline: Atari Sends Arcade Names to Rival Machines
body: Atari is treating its famous game catalog as portable property. COMPUTE! reports 12 releases under the ATARISOFT label for competing computers and consoles, carrying familiar arcade names beyond Atari hardware.

The strategy arrives as the console trade remains unsettled. Software sales on Commodore, Apple and Coleco machines give Atari another route to customers and acknowledge that a valuable game can outlive the box it first called home.
April’s Computer Entertainer tracks a busy field that includes B.C.’s Quest for Tires, Oil’s Well and Fathom. The shelf is fragmented, but the appetite for recognizable games remains strong.

stories.headline: PCjr and Macintosh Court the Newcomer
body: IBM and Apple are offering sharply different invitations to first-time buyers. The PCjr leans on the IBM name and PC family, while Macintosh asks users to learn a mouse-driven graphical vocabulary.
PCjr starts at $669, with the enhanced introduction configuration at $1,269; Macintosh arrives at $2,495. Price matters, but software support, expansion and the feel of daily work may matter more.

Early criticism of PCjr’s keyboard and limits gives Apple an opening, while IBM’s enormous software orbit remains a formidable advantage. The newcomer’s contest is already proving this week’s larger point: programs decide the value of the package.
